This vignette writes out every log-likelihood that ppnet evaluates and sets
each one beside its counterpart in the HawkesNet paper and in the hawkesNet R
package (github.com/duncan-clark/hawkesNet, `main` branch, commit `6aa26b8`).
The paper is

> Clark, D. A., Kresin, C. J. and Jones-Todd, C. M. (2026). A General Marked
> Point Process Framework For Self-Exciting Network Evolution. arXiv:2505.22659v2.
> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22659>

and equation, example and definition numbers below refer to that version.
Where the three differ, the difference is stated. Section 6 checks two of
the formulas numerically against ppnet.

Notation: events at times $t_1 < \dots < t_n$ in the window $[T_0, T)$,
$H_t$ the history before $t$, and $m_i$ the mark of event $i$ (the nodes and
edges it adds).

## 1. The common decomposition

All three use the marked point process log-likelihood (paper eq. 13) with
the intensity written as a ground rate times a mark PMF (paper eqs. 3 and 2),
$\lambda(t, m \mid H_t) = \lambda_g(t \mid H_t)\, q(m \mid t, H_t)$. Because
$q$ sums to one over the admissible marks, the compensator needs only the
ground rate (paper eq. 14), and

$$
\ell(\theta) = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \log q(m_i \mid t_i, H_{t_i})}_{\text{mark part}}
 + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \log \lambda_g(t_i \mid H_{t_i}) - \int_{T_0}^{T} \lambda_g(t \mid H_t)\,dt}_{\text{time part}}
\qquad \text{(paper eq. 15)}.
$$

In ppnet the two parts share no parameters, so `loglik(..., part = "time")`
and `loglik(..., part = "marks")` return them separately and
`fit_hawkesNet(..., part = )` fits them separately; the full log-likelihood
is their sum. hawkesNet evaluates the product $\lambda_g q$ at each event
and fits both parts together.

**What counts as an event.** In ppnet an event is a recorded event (an event
node in the bipartite data, or one arriving node in the unipartite data);
two events at the same time are two events, and the later one in the data
order sees the earlier one in its history. In hawkesNet an event is a
distinct time at which nodes or edges appear (`get_times()`), so updates at
the same time are merged into one event.

## 2. The time part

### Paper

The ground rate is a Hawkes-type kernel whose jumps may depend on past marks
and the graph (paper eq. 16), and for the examples the purely temporal
exponential kernel
$$
\lambda_g(t) = \lambda_\emptyset + K \sum_{t_j < t} e^{-\beta (t - t_j)},
\qquad
\int_0^T \lambda_g(t)\,dt = \lambda_\emptyset T + \frac{K}{\beta} \sum_{j=1}^n \left(1 - e^{-\beta (T - t_j)}\right)
\qquad \text{(paper eq. 17)}.
$$
$K/\beta$ is the branching ratio (expected direct offspring per event).

### hawkesNet

The same kernel, with `mu` $= \lambda_\emptyset$, `K` and `beta_overall`
$= \beta$. Optionally the constant $\lambda_\emptyset$ is replaced by a
kernel density estimate of the event times, fixed before fitting
(`prepare_inhomogeneous_background()`, `fit_hawkesNet_inhom()`). The
compensator is computed with the window length $T - T_0$ in place of $T$ in
eq. 17, so it is correct when the window starts at 0.

### ppnet

$$
\lambda_g(t) = \mu(t) + K \sum_{t_j < t} g_j\, e^{-\beta (t - t_j)}
 + K_f \sum_{t_j < t} e^{-\beta_f (t - t_j)},
$$
with three optional extensions; with all of them off it is paper eq. 17 with
`mu` $= \lambda_\emptyset$.

* **Time-varying baseline** (`baseline_spec()`):
  $\mu(t) = \mu \exp\{x(t)^\top b\}$, where $x(t)$ holds an optional linear
  trend and Fourier terms $\cos(2\pi h t / P), \sin(2\pi h t / P)$ for each
  period $P$ and harmonic $h$. Its integral is computed by Gauss-Legendre
  quadrature. This is a parametric alternative to hawkesNet's KDE
  background; its coefficients are estimated with the rest.
* **Two-scale kernel** (`kernel = "exp2"`): a second, faster exponential
  component ($K_f$ = `K_fast`, $\beta_f$ = `beta_fast` $> \beta$) with unit
  jumps. Its compensator adds
  $\frac{K_f}{\beta_f}\sum_j (1 - e^{-\beta_f (T - t_j)})$.
* **Mark-dependent jumps** (`excitation_spec()`, bipartite data only):
  $g_j = n_j^{\alpha} \exp\{\gamma\, h(c_j)\}$, with $n_j$ the number of
  perps at event $j$, $c_j$ the number of distinct earlier events sharing a
  perp with it (within `connectedness_window`, beyond
  `connectedness_min_gap`) and $h = \log(1 + \cdot)$ or the identity. This
  is a case of paper eq. 16, where the kernel may depend on past marks; the
  paper's own examples do not use it. $\alpha = \gamma = 0$ gives $g_j = 1$.
  The compensator's kernel term becomes
  $\frac{K}{\beta}\sum_j g_j (1 - e^{-\beta (T - t_j)})$.
* **Mark-path dependent jumps** (`excitation_spec(path_dependent = TRUE)`):
  $c_j(t)$ also counts the later events before $t$ that share a perp with
  event $j$, so an event's jump changes after it happens, as in the paper's
  mark path dependent Hawkes process (Definition 4.1, eq. 7). Each change at
  a later event $k$ is equivalent to an extra jump
  $(g_j^{\text{new}} - g_j^{\text{old}})\, e^{-\beta (t_k - t_j)}$ at $t_k$,
  so the likelihood stays an exact $O(n + \text{links})$ recursion.

All terms are computed by the usual $O(n)$ recursion
$S_k = e^{-\beta (t_k - t_{k-1})}(S_{k-1} + g_{k-1})$.

## 3. The mark part in the paper

**Example 1, preferential attachment (paper eq. 4).** Each event adds one
node and $K_t \sim \text{Poisson}(m)$ edges (capped at $N_{t-}$) from it to
existing nodes, chosen with probabilities
$p_i = \delta_i / \sum_k \delta_k$, $\delta_i = e^{-\tau (t - t_i)}\, d_i$
($d_i$ the degree of node $i$ just before $t$). Sampling without replacement
is approximated by independent Bernoulli terms:
$$
q(m_t) = P(K_t \mid m) \prod_{i=1}^{N_{t-}} p_i^{e_i} (1 - p_i)^{1 - e_i}.
$$

**Example 2, change statistics (paper eqs. 5, 6).** $N^{new}_t \sim
\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ new nodes, $K_t \sim \text{Poisson}(m)$ edges,
chosen from the candidates $C_t$ (pairs of a new and an existing node) with
weights
$w_{ij} = e^{-\tau (t - t_i)}\, \text{logit}^{-1}(\theta^\top C_{ij})$, with
$t_i$ the time of node $i$'s most recent activity and $C_{ij}$ the change
statistics of adding edge $(i, j)$. With $p^{CS}_{ij}$ the normalised weight,
$$
q(m_t) = \text{Poisson}(N^{new}_t; \lambda)\, \text{Poisson}(K_t; m)
 \prod_{(i,j) \in C_t} (p^{CS}_{ij})^{e_{ij}} (1 - p^{CS}_{ij})^{1 - e_{ij}}.
$$

## 4. The mark part in hawkesNet

**`PMF_mark_BA`** follows Example 1 with these differences:

* $t_i$ is node $i$'s entrance (birth) time.
* With `truncation`, only the most recent nodes (by entrance, or by latest
  activity with `mark_decay = "activity"`) are candidates, but the
  denominator $\sum_k \delta_k$ still runs over all existing nodes.
* $K_t$ is not capped in the density: the term is
  $\text{Poisson}(K_{obs}; m)$.
* A node with no edges yet has $\delta_i = 0$; a link to it gets probability
  `.Machine$double.eps` (about $2 \times 10^{-16}$) instead of 0.
* While the network has at most 2 nodes only the Poisson term is used.

**`PMF_mark_CS`** differs from Example 2 more:

* The Bernoulli probabilities are not normalised:
  $p_{ij} = \text{logit}^{-1}(\theta^\top C_{ij})\, e^{-\tau \Delta_{ij}}$.
* There is no $\text{Poisson}(K_t; m)$ term unless the parameters contain
  `m`; if they do, the term is added on top of the Bernoulli product (so the
  number of edges enters twice).
* With the default `mark_decay = "node_entrance"`, $\Delta_{ij}$ is the time
  since the older node's entrance; with `"activity"`, the time since the more
  recent of the two endpoints' latest activity (the paper's choice uses
  node $i$'s most recent activity).
* Candidates are all pairs among the `truncation` most recent nodes (both
  may be old) unless `growth_only = TRUE`, which keeps pairs with a new node.
* Change statistics come from ernm on the network with the event's new nodes
  added and none of its edges, so statistics that need two of the new edges
  (e.g. triangles through a new node) are 0.
* The node term is $\text{Poisson}(N^{new}_t; \lambda)$ (`node_lambda`).
* When the parameters have no `m`, R's partial matching makes `params$m`
  return `mu`, which switches the Poisson term on with mean $\mu$ (issue
  #11 on github.com/duncan-clark/hawkesNet). Until it is fixed, a fixed
  parameter whose name starts with "m" (e.g. `m_off`) avoids it.

Both PMFs can also include a multinomial term for categorical attributes of
new nodes (`vertex_categorical`).

## 5. The mark part in ppnet

ppnet has the unipartite models of the paper (`mark_type = "ba"`, `"cs"`)
and bipartite event-perp models (`"ba_bip"`, `"cs_bip"`, and `"ba_bip"` with
an `attachment_spec()`), which the paper does not cover.

### Unipartite

**`"ba"`.** Each event adds exactly one node. Existing node $i$ is joined
with probability
$$
p_i = \frac{w_i}{\sum_k w_k}, \qquad w_i = (2 d_i + \delta)\, e^{-\beta_e (t - b_i)},
$$
with $b_i$ its birth time and $\delta = 0.001$ (fixed), as independent
Bernoulli terms. The factor 2 (from `sna::degree()` on an undirected
network, as in hawkesNet) cancels except against $\delta$. There is no
$\text{Poisson}(K_t; m)$ term and no $m$: the probabilities sum to one, so
about one edge per event is expected.

**`"cs"`.** $M_t \sim \text{Poisson}$(`node_lambda`) new nodes; candidates
are the pairs of a new node and one of the `truncation` most recent
existing nodes;
$p = \text{logit}^{-1}(\theta^\top C)\, e^{-\beta_e (t - b_{old})}$
(not normalised), with $b_{old}$ the existing node's birth time and change
statistics from ernm (parameters `CS_<statistic>`). There is no
$\text{Poisson}(K_t; m)$ term.

### Bipartite

Each event adds one event node, $N^{new}$ new perps (each joined to it) and
edges to some of the existing ("old") perps. The mark PMF is
$P(\text{which old perps join})\, P(N^{new} \mid \text{old})$.

**`"ba_bip"` (original).** Old perp $v$ joins with probability
$p_v = w_v / \sum_u w_u$, $w_v = (2 d_v + \delta) e^{-\beta_e (t - b_v)}$,
$d_v$ the number of events it has attended, $b_v$ its first appearance,
$\delta = 0.001$; $N^{new} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{new})$. As for
`"ba"`, about one old perp is expected per event.

**`"cs_bip"`.** Old perp $v$ joins with probability
$\text{logit}^{-1}(\theta^\top C_v)\, e^{-\beta_e (t - b_v)}$, change
statistics from ernm; $N^{new} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{new})$.

**`"ba_bip"` with `attachment_spec()`.** The main bipartite model. Old perp
$v$ has weight
$$
\log w_v = \log(d_v + \delta) + \theta\, x_v + \theta_p\, y_v + \theta_r\, r_v
 - \beta_e (t_k - \ell_v),
$$
with $\ell_v$ the time of $v$'s latest event (not its first), and
change statistics from $v$'s own history (each term optional):
$x_v = h$(distinct co-offenders, `coffenders`),
$y_v = h$(3-paths $k - v - j - u$, i.e. co-offenders with multiplicity,
`paths`), both within `coffender_window`, and $r_v = h$(own events within
the episode gap, `recent`). It joins independently with probability
$$
p_v = 1 - \exp(-m\, w_v / W), \qquad W = \sum_u w_u,
$$
so `m` is close to the expected number of returning perps when the $p_v$ are
small: unlike the original BA models, the number of returning perps is a
parameter, as $m$ is in the paper. The new perps are $\text{Poisson}$ or
negative binomial (`new_perps`), and with `min_perps = 1` an event with no
old perp has $1 + N^{new}$ perps with its own rate (`lambda_new0`).

* **Random effect** (`random_effect = TRUE`): $p_v = 1 - \exp(-u_v m w_v /
  W)$ with $u_v \sim \text{Gamma}(1/\sigma^2, 1/\sigma^2)$, integrated out
  perp by perp: in closed form,
  $(1 + \sigma^2 Q_v)^{-1/\sigma^2}$ with $Q_v = \sum_k m w_{vk}/W_k$, for a
  perp that never returns, and by Gauss-Legendre quadrature in $\log u_v$
  otherwise. This is a marginal likelihood over the perps' propensities.
* **4-cycles** (`cycles = TRUE`): joins at the same event depend on each
  other through $z_{vk}$, the 4-cycles $k - v - j - u - k$ that $v$ joining
  closes (past events $j$ shared with another old perp $u$ at $k$). Each
  old perp is scored by its full conditional given the others,
  $\text{logit}\, P(v \mid \text{rest}) = \log(e^{m w_v / W} - 1) +
  \theta_c z_{vk} (+ \theta_{cs} z^s_{vk})$, and the product of these is a
  **pseudo-likelihood**, not a likelihood; with the 4-cycle coefficients at 0
  it is the model above exactly. Standard errors come from the sandwich
  (`attachment_vcov()`, or `vcov()` on the fit), and `logLik()`, `AIC()` and
  `anova()` refuse these fits.

All these are exact Bernoulli products over the old perps (no
without-replacement approximation is involved, as joins are independent by
construction), evaluated in time linear in events and perp appearances.

## 6. Two checks

The time part of a plain fit is paper eq. 17. Computed directly:

```{r}
library(ppnet)
set.seed(1)
p <- list(mu = 1, K = 0.5, beta = 1.2, beta_edges = 0.3, lambda_new = 0.7)
ev <- sim_hawkesNet(p, T_end = 30, mark_type = "ba_bip")$ev
t <- ev$times$t
T_end <- 30

lambda_at <- vapply(seq_along(t), function(i) {
  p$mu + p$K * sum(exp(-p$beta * (t[i] - t[seq_len(i - 1)])))
}, numeric(1))
eq17 <- sum(log(lambda_at)) -
  (p$mu * T_end + p$K / p$beta * sum(1 - exp(-p$beta * (T_end - t))))

c(eq17 = eq17, ppnet = loglik(ev, p, mark_type = "ba_bip", T_end = T_end, part = "time"))
```

The attachment model's mark part, computed directly for a model with degree
and recency only (each old perp's weight, then the Bernoulli terms and the
Poisson term for new perps), against ppnet:

```{r}
spec <- attachment_spec()                    # degree and recency
pm <- list(m = 0.8, beta_edges = 0.3, delta = 0.5, lambda_new = 0.7)

ev_nodes <- ev$nodes
ev_edges <- ev$edges
role <- setNames(ev_nodes$role, ev_nodes$id)
ll <- 0
deg <- c(); last <- c()                      # by perp id
for (k in seq_len(nrow(ev$times))) {
  id_k <- ev$times$event_id[k]
  t_k <- ev$times$t[k]
  e_k <- ev_edges[ev_edges$event_id == id_k, ]
  perps_k <- unique(c(e_k$i, e_k$j)[role[as.character(c(e_k$i, e_k$j))] == "perp"])
  old <- names(deg)
  if (length(old)) {
    w <- (deg + pm$delta) * exp(-pm$beta_edges * (t_k - last))
    pj <- 1 - exp(-pm$m * w / sum(w))
    joined <- old %in% as.character(perps_k)
    ll <- ll + sum(log(ifelse(joined, pj, 1 - pj)))
  }
  new <- setdiff(as.character(perps_k), old)
  ll <- ll + dpois(length(new), pm$lambda_new, log = TRUE)
  for (v in as.character(perps_k)) {
    deg[v] <- if (v %in% names(deg)) deg[v] + 1 else 1
    last[v] <- t_k
  }
}
c(direct = ll, ppnet = loglik(ev, pm, mark_type = "ba_bip", attachment = spec,
                              T_end = T_end, part = "marks"))
```

The package tests (`tests/testthat/`) check every likelihood above against
an independent brute-force calculation in the same way, including the
excitation, path-dependent, 3-path, 4-cycle, episode-gap and random-effect
terms, and their analytic gradients against finite differences.

## 7. Summary

| | Paper | hawkesNet (`main`) | ppnet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Event | update time | distinct time (ties merged) | recorded event (ties kept) |
| Ground rate | $\lambda_\emptyset + K\sum e^{-\beta\Delta}$ (eq. 17), marks allowed (eq. 16) | eq. 17; or KDE background | eq. 17, plus log-linear seasonal/trend baseline, fast second kernel, size/connectedness jumps, path-dependent jumps |
| Compensator | closed form | closed form, window assumed to start at 0 | closed form (quadrature for the baseline) |
| BA mark | Poisson($m$) edges $\times$ normalised degree-decay Bernoullis | as paper; decay from birth; truncation; uncapped Poisson | `"ba"`: normalised $(2d+\delta)$-decay Bernoullis, no $m$ |
| CS mark | Poisson nodes $\times$ Poisson($m$) edges $\times$ normalised logistic-decay Bernoullis | unnormalised Bernoullis; Poisson nodes; no $m$ term unless given (then added on top); `m`/`mu` partial-match bug | `"cs"`: unnormalised Bernoullis, Poisson nodes, new-old candidates, no $m$ |
| Bipartite | — | — (`pre-jasa-main` branch only) | `"ba_bip"`, `"cs_bip"`; attachment model with $m$, own-history change statistics, NB new perps, random effect, 4-cycles (pseudo-likelihood) |
| Optimiser | Nelder–Mead | Nelder–Mead (default), numerical | BFGS with analytic gradients |
| Standard errors | Hessian or parametric bootstrap | Hessian | Hessian (delta method to the natural scale); sandwich for pseudo-likelihood |
